questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: The history of the first vaccines
The possibility of a vaccine that helps the body fight cancer
Why chemotherapy is the best cancer treatment
How to avoid getting cancer
questions.why: They find out whether a vaccine for cancer could soon become a reality.

questions.q: According to Beth, how many people will be affected by cancer in their lifetime?
options: 1 in 2
1 in 10
1 in 50
1 in 5
questions.why: Beth says in our lifetime 1 in 5 people will be affected by cancer.

questions.q: Why does Beth say 'we'll be focusing on some good news instead'?
options: Because the facts about cancer deaths she has just given are sad
Because the number of cancer deaths is now falling very quickly worldwide
Because most tumours are not cancerous
Because a cure has already been found
questions.why: She mentions 9.7 million cancer deaths in 2022, then turns to the positive news about vaccines.

questions.q: According to Dr Meredith McKean, why doesn't the immune system fight cancer by itself?
options: Cancer cells grow far too slowly for the immune system to notice them
The immune system only fights viruses
Cancer cells send signals telling the immune system to go away
Cancer cells are too small to see
questions.why: She says cancer puts signals on its surface telling the immune system, 'Go away! There's nothing here.'

questions.q: What has understanding these cancer signals led to?
options: A breakthrough in immune therapy over the past ten years
A new type of chemotherapy that is much safer for patients
A test that finds cancer at birth
The end of all cancer research
questions.why: She says it has 'really allowed a breakthrough with immune therapy over the past decade'.

questions.q: What is the problem with treatments like chemotherapy?
options: They are too slow to work
They only work on benign tumours and not on the cancerous, malignant ones
They also attack healthy tissue and cause unpleasant side effects
They make the cancer spread faster
questions.why: Neil says they target cancer but also attack healthy tissue, creating unpleasant side effects.

questions.q: How are the new cancer vaccines different?
options: They can only be given to healthy people
They replace the immune system completely
They destroy every cell in the tumour area, both healthy and cancerous
They train the immune system to attack only cancer cells
questions.why: They retrain the immune system to recognise and eliminate cancer cells, 'and only those'.

questions.q: What does Professor Eduardo Sanchez say vaccines need to do?
options: Make cancer cells grow more slowly
Teach the immune system again to recognise cancer cells
Help the cancer cells to hide more successfully from the body's defences
Make the immune system rest
questions.why: He says the immune system has forgotten how to recognise cancer, so vaccines must 're-educate' it.
